hero.kicker: We tested the tricks your coaching centre teaches
hero.claim: Fifteen elimination rules, 1,400 real questions, one official answer key. One rule works — and it stopped working in 2022.
hero.body: “Statements with ‘only’ are almost never correct” is taught everywhere and is right 43% of the time, not the 1–5% the handbooks claim. Every rule here carries the rate at which it is actually right, measured against the key rather than asserted.

skipped.noStatements: This question prints no numbered statements, so the answer key cannot say which claim is true and no rule can be checked on it.
skipped.partialCount: This is a “how many of the above” question: the key pins how many statements are correct, never which, so nothing here can be checked.
skipped.negativePolarity: This question asks which statements are NOT correct, which inverts the mapping. Excluded rather than risk labelling a statement backwards.
skipped.unkeyed: This question was dropped by UPSC, so it carries no official answer.
skipped.noEnglish: No English text was extracted for this question.
skipped.notStatements: The options name things rather than referring to numbered statements, so the key cannot label the statements.
skipped.misprinted: The options refer to a statement that is not printed on the page, so the key cannot be trusted to label them.
skipped.unknown: This question cannot be decoded into statement-level truth.

eliminationPage.title: Elimination Lab
eliminationPage.lede: Every option-elimination shortcut taught on the coaching circuit, measured against fourteen years of keyed Prelims questions. Turn the Lab on in the header and every question page will show what these rules would have told you, beside the official answer.
eliminationPage.methodBaseline: The baseline is not 50%. UPSC writes more true statements than false ones, and each question's true-count is already fixed by its answer key, so each rule is scored against a per-question hypergeometric null rather than a flat rate.
eliminationPage.methodBonferroni: Fifteen rules are tested at once, so the significance threshold is Bonferroni-corrected. Testing fifteen things at the usual 0.05 produces one 'pattern' by construction.
eliminationPage.methodDirection: The rate shown is how often the marked statement is TRUE. An elimination rule that works shows a rate below its baseline.
eliminationPage.methodUntestable: Claims about examiner psychology, cognitive overload and etymology are not listed: they are assertions about intent, and nothing in a printed paper can decide them.

trends.title: How the paper has changed
trends.lede: The mix of question types, year by year, across every published Prelims paper. Counting only — no model is involved in either chart.
trends.footnote: UPSC changed how it builds Prelims questions in 2022: the “How many of the above are correct?” format went from zero occurrences to roughly a fifth of the paper. A statistic pooled across that break describes an exam nobody is sitting, which is why every analysis in this product is split at 2022.

patterns.title: Does the answer leak?
patterns.lede: Four beliefs about how UPSC builds its options — the same letter recurring, the odd one out, the unfamiliar three, options carrying dates — tested against every question with an official answer key.
patterns.letterNote: Chi-square against a uniform spread: p = {p}. A p above 0.05 means the letters are as evenly spread as chance would make them.
patterns.archetypeNote: This is why the baseline is not 25%: where the options are “1 only / 2 only / Both 1 and 2 / Neither 1 nor 2”, “Both 1 and 2” is mechanically the longest string. Rates are compared against a null built by permuting which option is correct within each of these families.
patterns.recurrenceTitle: What does repeat: the questions themselves
patterns.recurrenceLede: Questions on the same topic whose meaning sits close together are, in practice, the same archetype asked twice. This is measured on the embeddings the corpus already carries — and unlike the option patterns above, it is real and uneven.
patterns.curveItem: questions have a twin at {threshold} similarity
patterns.footnote: Five hypotheses are tested at once, so the significance threshold is corrected for the family. “Not a usable signal” is the useful answer here, not a failure: a shortcut that fires at chance is worth knowing does not work before you spend an exam on it.

depth.title: How deeply this topic has been probed
depth.lede: Where the questions have actually landed inside this topic, which years it skipped, and which of its branches have never been asked from.
depth.notClassified: The format and cognitive-depth mixes need the classification pass, which has not run. Only what is derivable from the printed page is shown.
depth.repeats: Questions that rhyme with an earlier one
depth.repeatsNote: Same topic, near-identical meaning. Measured on embeddings, not a model's opinion.
depth.projectionLede: Projected from the measured mix of comparable topics, never from a model's speculation. It says how topics like this one are examined — not what will be asked.
depth.expectedVolume: Comparable topics carry about {rate} questions a year.
depth.untouched: {count} branch(es) here have never been asked from: {names}.

practice.title: Sit a paper
practice.lede: Real UPSC questions with the official answer key behind them, scored the way UPSC scores: full marks for a correct answer, a third off for a wrong one, nothing either way for a blank.
practice.yearBody: One year exactly as it was printed, in printed order. A score here is comparable to what anyone else scored on that paper.
practice.mockBody: {count} questions sampled across every year in the corpus, {minutes} minutes.
practice.drillBody: Every keyed question on one topic and everything under it. Shorter, and not comparable to a full paper — this is recall practice, not a rehearsal.
practice.notEnough: Not enough keyed questions in the corpus for that selection yet. Try another topic, or a mixed mock.
practice.noPapers: No complete keyed paper is ingested yet.
practice.footnote: Nothing here is generated. Every question is a real question from a real paper, and every answer comes from the official UPSC key — a question UPSC dropped is never put on a scored paper.

practice.negativeMarking: A wrong answer costs a third of a mark. A blank costs nothing.
